issues.description: The problem statement requires the SealSaloon.orders attribute to be a modifiable List<Meal>, but the reference solution implements orders as a Meal[] array. This mismatch between the specified data structure (List) and the solution (array) is structural and can confuse students about which type to implement. The rest of the template code (ArrayHelpers, Stock) uses arrays, which suggests arrays may have been intended, but the problem text explicitly asks for a List<Meal>.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the specification and template consistent: either (A) change the problem statement and UML to require an array-based orders field (Meal[] orders) to match the provided ArrayHelpers and the reference solution, or (B) update the reference solution and any helper code to use a modifiable List<Meal> for orders (and adjust checkOrderReady, orderMeal, calculateRemainingOrderNumber to use List APIs). Ensure the problem statement, UML, template examples, and solution all use the same orders type.

issues.description: The problem statement requires a modifiable List<Meal> attribute named 'orders', but the provided codebase (template/solution) consistently uses arrays (Meal[]) for order storage and helper utilities (ArrayHelpers, Stock use arrays). This mismatch between the described collection type (List) and the implemented type (array) creates a conceptual mapping burden: students will look for List-based APIs and may be confused by array-based helpers and the solution which uses Meal[].
issues.suggestedFix: Make the collection type consistent across artifacts. Either update the problem statement to request an array-based 'orders' field (Meal[]) and reference the ArrayHelpers utilities, or refactor the template and solution to use java.util.List<Meal> (e.g., ArrayList) for 'orders' and replace array helper usage with List operations.
